description: Five questions on Big-O and searching. Questions 4a and 4b are variants; each student sees one.

questions.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search on an unsorted array of n elements?

options.rationale: In the worst case the target is last or absent, so all n elements are checked.
Confuses linear search with binary search, which needs a sorted array.
Describes the best case (target is first), not the worst case.
Mixes in the cost of sorting first; linear search does not sort.

questions.stem: A loop runs `for i in range(n)` and, inside it, `for j in range(n)`. Each inner step does constant work. What is the total time complexity?

options.rationale: Counts only the outer loop and ignores that the inner loop runs n times per outer step.
Adds the loops instead of multiplying them; nested loops multiply.
The inner loop runs n times for each of n outer iterations: n x n = n^2 steps.
Logarithmic time needs the problem size to shrink by a factor each step, which does not happen here.

questions.stem: Which condition must hold before binary search can be used on an array?

options.text: The array contains no duplicate values
options.rationale: Binary search works with duplicates; it may just find any one of them.

options.text: The array length is a power of two
options.rationale: Midpoints are rounded, so any length works.

options.text: The array is stored in contiguous memory
options.rationale: Random access helps performance, but the required condition is ordering.

options.text: The array is sorted by the search key
options.rationale: Discarding half the array each step is only valid if the elements are in order.

questions.stem: Binary search looks for 15 in the sorted array below, using mid = (low + high) // 2 with indices starting at 0. Which values are compared with 15, in order?

options.rationale: Traces a linear search from the start instead of a binary search.
After the first comparison, steps one position left instead of recomputing mid = (0 + 2) // 2 = 1.
After setting high = 2, scans the remaining half from its start instead of recomputing the midpoint.

questions.stem: Binary search looks for 61 in the sorted array below, using mid = (low + high) // 2 with indices starting at 0. Which values are compared with 61, in order?

options.rationale: Moves low to 4 but then compares index 4 instead of recomputing mid = (4 + 6) // 2 = 5.
Starts at index 4 by using the 1-based middle position (7 // 2 + 1) instead of mid = (0 + 6) // 2 = 3.
Skips the second midpoint, as if the search jumped to the last element after one comparison.

questions.stem: An algorithm halves the remaining input on every step until one element is left. Roughly how many steps does it take for an input of 1,024 elements?

options.rationale: Halves the input once and reports the remaining size instead of counting steps.
Counts one step per element, which is linear behavior.
Takes the square root of 1,024 instead of the base-2 logarithm.
1,024 = 2^10, so halving reaches one element after log2(1,024) = 10 steps.
